note: Lesson explanations are written by the CTRL+SPACE team. Every statement about NASA results is backed by the listed passage IDs from corpus.json. Explanations are teaching aids, not primary evidence.

lessons.title: Why fire behaves differently in microgravity
lessons.summary: Buoyancy, why long-duration tests on the ISS matter, and why Earth-based material tests may not be enough.

sections.heading: Buoyancy on Earth
sections.explanation: On Earth, hot combustion gases are lighter than the surrounding air, so they rise and pull fresh air towards the flame. In microgravity this buoyant flow is greatly reduced, so the air reaching a flame comes mainly from ventilation fans or the experiment’s own flow. The exact effect depends on the experiment and its conditions.

sections.heading: Why the ISS?
sections.explanation: Drop towers only give a few seconds of microgravity. NASA’s BASS-II team argued that longer microgravity time is needed to study flammability limits for anything thicker than very thin films.

sections.heading: A hypothesis, not a result
sections.explanation: The BASS-II team stated as a hypothesis that, with enough ventilation, materials may burn more readily in microgravity than in normal gravity. Treat it as a question the experiments set out to test.

sections.heading: One measured example
sections.explanation: For one ¼” PMMA rod, steady spreading was seen in BASS-II at a lower oxygen level than the normal-gravity blowoff limit. The authors concluded that, for this material, normal-gravity limits should be de-rated. This is one material and one geometry, not a rule for every material.

objectives: Explain why buoyant flow is weak in microgravity
Tell a hypothesis apart from a measured result
Describe the BASS-II oxygen margin-of-safety finding and its limits

lessons.title: Airflow, quenching and blow-off
lessons.summary: How very low and very high airflow can both put a flame out.

sections.heading: Two ways to go out
sections.explanation: In BASS-II thin PMMA tests, flames quenched by radiative losses when the flow became very slow, and approached blow-off when the flow became fast.

sections.heading: The flammability boundary
sections.explanation: The SMMRF investigation found the lowest point of the PMMA flammability boundary at very low flows, close to diffusive flows. As oxygen drops, the flow needed to blow the flame off also becomes slower.

sections.heading: Fabric in concurrent flow
sections.explanation: Growth and Extinction Limit tests on SIBAL fabric recorded six quenching cases as flow was reduced and one blow-off case as flow was increased.

objectives: Name the two extinction modes seen in BASS-II
Explain where the PMMA flammability boundary has its minimum
Relate fabric quenching cases to reduced flow

lessons.title: Oxygen concentration and flame spread
lessons.summary: What BASS-II tests reported about oxygen, and how oxygen was controlled in the glovebox.

sections.heading: Controlling oxygen on orbit
sections.explanation: BASS-II lowered oxygen by diluting the glovebox atmosphere with nitrogen, from ambient ISS levels down to about 14% for near-limit flames.

sections.heading: Spread rate and oxygen
sections.explanation: In the Material Ignition and Suppression Test, averaged over all flow velocities, flame spread rate on PMMA rods rose as oxygen increased in microgravity.

sections.heading: Diameter and gravity
sections.explanation: The same investigation reported lower spread rates for thicker rods, and higher spread rates in normal gravity than in microgravity for these samples.

objectives: Describe how BASS-II lowered oxygen on orbit
State the reported trend of spread rate with oxygen
Avoid generalising one material’s trend to all materials

lessons.title: Combustion products in a closed spacecraft
lessons.summary: Heat release, carbon monoxide and fuel-rich flames from BASS-II and Saffire VI.

sections.heading: Small flames, measurable products
sections.explanation: Most BASS-II flames released well below 100 W, and heat release tended to increase with ambient oxygen.

sections.heading: Incomplete combustion
sections.explanation: The CO-to-CO2 ratio in BASS-II was about an order of magnitude above efficient flue gases, and the flames were estimated to burn fuel rich on average.

sections.heading: At spacecraft scale
sections.explanation: In the large Saffire VI tests aboard a Cygnus spacecraft, the rise in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide was more significant than the temperature and pressure rise.

objectives: Interpret heat release rates of small microgravity flames
Explain what a high CO/CO2 ratio indicates
Compare product build-up with temperature rise in Saffire VI

lessons.title: Opposed and concurrent flame spread
lessons.summary: Two flow configurations that experiments keep separate, and why you shouldn’t mix them in comparisons.

sections.heading: With or against the wind
sections.explanation: Concurrent flames spread in the same direction as the airflow; opposed flames spread against it. BASS-II tested both because they represent different real fire situations.

sections.heading: Examples in the data
sections.explanation: The Narrow Channel Validation tests were all opposed flow, while SMMRF rods and Saffire VI samples burned in concurrent flow.

sections.heading: Comparing fairly
sections.explanation: Because the configurations differ, CTRL+SPACE warns you when a comparison mixes opposed and concurrent experiments.

objectives: Define opposed and concurrent flame spread
Identify which experiments used each configuration
Explain why mixing them in a comparison needs a warning

challenges.title: The oxygen margin of safety
challenges.summary: Three questions on the BASS-II SMMRF result for PMMA rods.

questions.prompt: In BASS-II, steady flame spreading on the ¼” PMMA rod was observed at what oxygen level?
What was the normal-gravity (1g) blowoff limit for the same rod?
What did the authors conclude from the negative oxygen margin of safety?
options: Normal-gravity flammability limits should be de-rated
Oxygen has no effect on flame spread

challenges.objective: Interpret the BASS-II SMMRF result for ¼” PMMA rods.
challenges.background: A negative oxygen margin of safety means a material kept burning in microgravity below an oxygen level where it stopped in normal gravity.
challenges.instructions: Choose one answer per question, then submit. Answers are checked against the quoted NASA passage for each question, which is shown after you submit. Your unsent answers are saved on this device.

challenges.objective: Recall the flow conditions that ended or sustained flames in BASS-II and Saffire VI.
